qs.q: If $A_{n\times n}$ and $\det(A)\neq0$, then the reduced row-echelon form of $A$ ----
e: By the equivalence theorem for an $n\times n$ matrix: $\det(A)\neq0\iff A$ is invertible $\iff$ the reduced row-echelon form of $A$ is $I_n$.
So the reduced row-echelon form is always $I_n$.

qs.q: If $A$ and $B$ are two square matrices such that $\det(A)\det(B)=1$, then ----
e: $\det(A)\det(B)=\det(AB)=1\neq0$ only tells us that $AB$ is invertible. It does not force $AB=I$.
Example where $A\neq B^{-1}$: $A=I$, $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$. Then $\det A\det B=1$, but $B^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\neq A$.
Both cases occur, so $A$ may be equal to $B^{-1}$.
A matrix is invertible iff its determinant is nonzero, so $AB$ is not invertible.

qs.q: $A$ is a square matrix. If the linear system $AX=b$ has only one solution, then $\det(A)$ ----
e: By the equivalence theorem: $AX=b$ has exactly one solution $\iff A$ is invertible $\iff\det(A)\neq0$.

qs.q: If $A$ is a square matrix such that $\det(2A)\neq0$, then $A$ ----

e: A square matrix is invertible iff its determinant is nonzero. $\det(A)=\det(B)\neq0$, so both $A$ and $B$ are invertible.
$A=B$ is not forced: take $A=I$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$. Both have determinant $1$ but $A\neq B$.
(The original exam also listed a third choice, 'AB is invertible', which is also true because $\det(AB)=\det A\det B\neq0$. It was removed here so that only one choice is correct.)

e: $AX=0$ always has the trivial solution $X=0$. If it is the only solution, then $A$ is invertible (equivalence theorem).
Choices (a) and (c) are wrong because they allow $\det(A)=0$.

qs.q: If $A$ and $B$ are two matrices such that $\det(AB^{-1})\neq0$, then ----
e: $AB^{-1}$ has a determinant, so it is square, and $B^{-1}$ exists, so $B$ is square and invertible. Hence $A$ is square as well.

qs.q: If $A_{3\times3}$ is a matrix such that $AX=0$ has infinity many solutions, then $\det(A)$ is ----
e: Infinitely many solutions means there is a nontrivial solution, so $A$ is not invertible.
Zero is neither positive nor negative.

qs.q: If $A$ is a square matrix and $\det(A^T)\neq0$, then the linear system $AX=0$ has ----
e: For an invertible matrix, $AX=0$ has only the trivial solution $X=0$ (equivalence theorem).
A homogeneous system always has a solution, so 'no solution' is impossible, and the unique solution is $X=0$.
